claims.text: A thin CrN interlayer can serve as a diffusion barrier between a zirconium-alloy substrate and an elemental Cr topcoat.
The CrN interlayer will suppress elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Suppressing Cr–Zr interdiffusion will preserve coating protection under normal subcritical-water reactor conditions.
Suppressing Cr–Zr interdiffusion will preserve coating protection during accident-relevant high-temperature steam exposure.
The proposed CrN interlayer thickness is approximately 1 µm.
Approximately 300°C represents the normal subcritical-water operating condition considered by the hypothesis.
Steam exposure up to approximately 1200°C represents the accident-relevant high-temperature condition considered by the hypothesis.
A dense CrN interlayer physically impedes atomic diffusion across the Cr/Zr interface.
The CrN barrier increases the activation energy for Cr–Zr interdiffusion at elevated temperatures.
Increasing the activation energy hinders migration of Cr and Zr atoms.
The CrN barrier prevents formation of brittle intermetallic phases at the coating–substrate interface.
Brittle intermetallic phases formed by Cr–Zr interdiffusion can compromise coating integrity.
Relative to standalone Cr-coated cladding, CrN-modified cladding will have a significantly smaller interdiffusion profile.
Relative to standalone Cr-coated cladding, CrN-modified cladding will exhibit improved oxidation resistance.
A standalone elemental Cr coating on zirconium-alloy cladding is vulnerable to interdiffusion-induced degradation at elevated temperatures.
The proposed protective effect is expected to persist at approximately 300°C and during steam exposure up to approximately 1200°C for durations on the order of hours.
Performance at longer durations or more extreme conditions is uncertain.
The long-term durability of CrN under cyclic thermal and environmental stress remains unvalidated.
